utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. I think we are hearing French on English channel. I think it has been corrected. Yes, Mr. Tieger, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I was also having some volume difficulties, but I think those are resolved. Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours and everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In paragraph 15 of your statement, you note that the SRK was mainly engaged in defensive operations and then provide a few details in connection with that assertion. I wanted to ask you a few questions about that. First of all, you mention Lukavac 93 as the only offensive operation that you recall, and in connection with our discussion on Thursday before we adjourned, I wanted to call that up briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's 65 ter 23948. And if we could turn to page 3 of the English and turn one more page in the B/C/S, please. And we'll need one more, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And directing your attention to item 2, Colonel, we see that among the objectives of Lukavac 93 was to prevent the unblocking of Sarajevo and create conditions for its take-over. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we zoom in a bit, please, because it's not very legible. The copy isn't very good. First of all, the heading of the document says that it's the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps document. I didn't see the year, whether it's 1993 or 1994. It wasn't quite clear --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, if you need us to return to the front page, we can do that. And I think for your purposes you'll want to read down to the bottom of page 3 and up to the top of page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But let's go back to the front page so the Colonel can see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's still not very clear, but that's not a problem. Let's go back to item number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So return to page 3 of the B/C/S toward the bottom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here it says the SRK acting together with two brigades from the 1st KK has the following task: Mount a decisive and active defence to prevent a breakthrough of the Muslim forces on the axis Rajlovac-Rajkovica-Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. And my question was whether or not one of the objectives of Lukavac 93 was to prevent the unblocking of Sarajevo and to create conditions for its takeover. So in that connection, if you could look to the bottom of page 3 and then read on to the top of page 4 to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's clear that the offensive was to prevent the unblocking of Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could go to the top of page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then -- yes, that was the SRK's objective, prevent the unblocking of Sarajevo, and Lukavica 93 had this objective, to join the SRK with the Herzegovina Corps in order to create good links with the south and south-eastern part of Republika Srpska. That was the purpose of Lukavica 93, and I -- it says prevent the unblocking of Sarajevo and join up with the Herzegovina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And I'll be asking you a couple of questions in a minute about the joining up of that region of the country, but I'd like to move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I could tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P5981, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, before the winter of 1992 there were efforts undertaken to secure and -- in the terms of the -- used by the VRS, liberate portions of what was considered to be Serbian territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before winter 1992, as far as I can remember, there was an attempt to liberate the road to Trnovo and to join up with -- the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps with the Herzegovina Corps. But nothing succeeded. Only Kijevo was liberated which is behind Sarajevo, behind Krupac. But no one continued in the direction of Trnovo, so that action wasn't successful as far as I remember. That was in the month of November or December.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By the beginning of the winter of 1992, there was -- the VRS did not consider that it had great need for offensive operations because it considered that it had achieved many of the military goals of the war and that much of the territory that was sought to be liberated had, in fact, been and was under control of the Bosnian Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the Main Staff of the VRS thought or the political leadership of Republika Srpska. So I don't know how I could answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn to P01005 momentarily, please. Okay. And we can turn -- this is a document dated the 9th of September, 1992. If -- it's issued by the SRK command, as you can see, and it indicates at the bottom of page 1: "As winter is around the corner and for the most part we have achieved the military goals of the war and do not expect major movements of the front line ..." turn to the next page, "along certain axes in our favour, which the commanders know ..." And then there is an order in accordance with that assessment. So, Colonel, this reflects the assessment of the SRK command that most of the military goals had been achieved and therefore the need for further offensive operations to obtain territory or for other purposes was no longer what it had been; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the SRK from the beginning of the war until the end, the lines didn't move on either of the sides. Only on certain axes the tactical position of our forces were improved or the positions of the Muslim forces. Since winter was approaching, it's obvious that this order was issued so that the troops could prepare for the winter. The winters are hard and cold in Sarajevo and it was necessary to protect the army from precipitation and low temperatures. And as a result, shelters were built and fuel was prepared for heating soldiers --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, I appreciate your attention to detail but we'll move a bit quicker if you can simply focus on my question. Just to give you an indication of that, I'm focusing on your comment that the operations were largely defensive and I wanted to get underneath that to see why, not to identify the preparations were made for winter. But thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would normally have tendered that, but it's in evidence, as you can see. I should note, however, that it was admitted as a source document, so now I think it should be admitted as any other document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for that notation. It will be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in connection with the objectives that P1005 refer to, it is correct that by -- that the Bosnian Serb military forces controlled approximately, if not more than, 70 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably, if that's what it says in the document. At that time that was probably the case as far as the SRK is concerned. As far as I know, in the field, from the very beginning of the war, the positions changed very little on both sides in the Sarajevo area. So there were no drastic changes when it comes to the positions of both the sides concerned and the objective was to maintain the blockade and to prevent the Muslim forces from breaking through from Sarajevo, and that's what I spoke about on Thursday and I told you about what this related to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, a moment ago you mentioned the interest in linking up with the Herzegovina Corps. It was -- it is correct, isn't it, that Lukavac 93 was aimed at, among other things, linking Herzegovina, the other parts of Republika Srpska, and therefore having a contiguous or unified or compact territory and thus achieving one of the broader goals of the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the main objective was to establish a link between the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the Herzegovina Corps, to have better communications between the south and south-eastern part of Republika Srpska and this was also the purpose of support, to facilitate command, and to make it easier for the VRS as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Maybe we're talking about the same thing in slightly different way, but in that connection let me turn to a couple of documents. First D00568, page 4 of the English and of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I can't read this document. I can't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll have that blown up for you in a second, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's fine now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And I'm directing your attention to what would be essentially the second paragraph. I think you can see the reference to Lukavac 93.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could split screen with the English so the Judges can see it in English, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we be told what this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm surprised the accused doesn't know that because he introduced it. It's a speech of Major-General Milosevic at the ceremony of presenting war flags.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And on that occasion General Milosevic said - and we can scroll up on the English, please: "Our entire struggle was somehow crowned by the 'Lukavac 93' operation that took place in the area of Jahorina, Treskavica, Bjelasnica, and Igman," et cetera, et cetera. And then he goes to say: "Soldiers were exceptionally motivated because we were achieving our strategic goal and that was the linking of Herzegovina to other part of RS because without that, we did not have a state."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And similarly, I would like to turn quickly to 65 ter 10743, page 37 of the English and page 18 of the B/C/S. That's an interview with -- lengthy serialised interview in "Nin" with General Mladic in 1994. And that is at page 18 of the B/C/S, page 37 of the English, please. And toward the bottom, please, in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, Colonel, I think you'll see the reference to Lukavac 93 in the middle of the page with the paragraph that begins: "From February until 27 July 1993 ..." And there General Mladic continues discussing Lukavac 93 at the -- we see at the bottom of the page in English. "This made it possible to join Herzegovina territorially --" and I'm quoting now: "This made it possible to join Herzegovina territorially with the Sarajevo-Romanija basin and to achieve another one of our strategic aims - unification of the regions of Republika Srpska." So, Colonel, I know when you were answering my question earlier you were speaking in terms of linking up the corps perhaps from military perspective, but it's correct, is it not, that one of the objectives of Lukavac 93 was achieving this broad strategic aim of unification of the regions of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that is what I said, something to that effect. Linking up, establishing a link between that part and the south part of or the south-eastern part of Republika Srpska, creating such a stretch of territory was an objective and it was also necessary to link up the corps in order to co-operate, provide support, and so on and so forth. But in any event, it was a matter of uniting ethnic areas where Serbs lived in order to make communications easier, co-operate more easily, and to maintain all communications, all linguist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would either tender that portion of 10743 or leave it to the Court if it considers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that it was read out, I'm asking you whether it's really necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I was noting that. I actually thought that might be the Court's view, so I'm satisfied. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, let me move on to a different subject. At a number of paragraphs in your statement, I think specifically 17, 20, and 29, you address some of the circumstances in which orders to use artillery were given and in which artillery fire was undertaken. So, for example, in paragraph 17 you refer to opening fire based on requests from adjoining 1st Motorised Brigade units, pursuant to an order or approval by the brigade or corps command on noticed artillery positions and enemy firing positions. In paragraph 20 you referred to those situations when you had to respond to observe firing positions -- to enemy fire from the town and observe firing positions and your selection of the most precise weapon. And in paragraph 29 you refer to the information that you acquired from observers and the details you demanded when there were shots from the depth of enemy territory, information that you say you required before you would consider authorising return fire. You again emphasise that you would select the weapon which was capable of the most precise fire. And I wanted to ask you some questions in connection with those paragraphs. First of all, by way of clarification, Colonel, when you referred to authorising return fire or selecting the most precise weapon, which of your roles that you described on Thursday were you referring to when you gave such authorisation or orders? In which capacity were you functioning when you referred to the circumstances reflected in these paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the chief of the artillery of the Sarajevo-Romanija Brigade in mind. I asked my subordinates, my professional subordinates, and they also requested this from their own men and they acted in this manner too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just so I understand exactly what you're saying here, are you suggesting in any way that this was limited to your efforts and that what you did was exceptional or anomalous or are you asserting that, as far as you were concerned, this was -- this reflected what the corps obligations and practices were?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can speak for myself as chief of the artillery. I was professionally responsible for the artillery in the 1st Sarajevo Brigade, and this concerned my acts and the acts of my subordinates and this was also requested by the command brigade. They requested this of me. When I was an official of the artillery, I had a chief of artillery who decided about everything. He was above me and I assisted him. I think the same procedure remained in place, it didn't change at the time, that concerns officials from the corps command and my chief of artillery.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I could just comment on the transcript. It doesn't say: When I was an official in the corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, do you confirm that, having said so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. When I was an official in the artillery organ of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me follow-up on a few of the points you make in that statement, then. First of all, you talk about selecting the most precise weapon and I take it that would be from the list of weapons that you provided earlier in your statement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'd like to ask you, then, under what circumstances you would use which of those weapons and what it was that would make one of those weapons the most precise weapon on one occasion but not the most precise weapon on another occasion. So let's start, for example, with mortars.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What weapons I would choose depended on the target itself, on the type of the target, the position of the target, as well as the position of the artillery assets and units and where they were. Bearing in mind the position of the target, the firing positions of the artillery weapons, you would choose the unit and the weapon that would be more precise in order to avoid unnecessary collateral damage and the destruction of civilian facilities, i.e., to bring the precision to a maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, there seems to be a suggestion there that on some occasions a mortar might be more precise, which I understand to mean more accurate in this context, than a howitzer and on some occasions more precise than a rocket, but on other occasions it would be different. Is that what you're saying or are you saying something else?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are targeting at sheltered targets, if they're on the last angle, it is impossible to target them with artillery weapons such as howitzers and cannon. They would miss and those targets would not be hit. A mortar is ideal for such targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And by a sheltered target, I take it you do not mean a protected, reinforced target, you mean something like a trench; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I had in mind was the configuration of the terrain. If a howitzer fires at it from the other side of the slope, it would overreach the target, whereas the mortar has a different trajectory and that's why it's more accurate on -- in firing targets on the bottom part of the slope as you're looking from our own positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let me ask the question in this way then: What types of targets are mortars good for? What are they intended for?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mortars are good to support our forward troops because they're more accurate, whereas the targets in front of the forward lines were mostly on the bottom part of the slope from our position and that's why mortars were more accurate in targeting those targets that directly threatened the positions of our units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, mortars are generally speaking anti-personnel weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. They're not intended as heavy weapons to blow up buildings; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not the intention. But they can be used to destroy trenches and inflicting losses to the troops as well as the destruction of some lighter structures belonging to the enemy side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But more specifically, for example, you wouldn't use a weapon against, for example, a reinforced command post, wouldn't do much good; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the reinforcement of the facility, how well reinforced it is. I wouldn't use mortars if shells are not supposed to achieve any effect due to the level of reinforcement of such a facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What about, for example, a sniper in a building, would a mortar have any significant utility there?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would never use those.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, I -- by the way, I wanted to ask you one thing before we began and that is: Looking at paragraphs 17, 20, and 29, there's an emphasis on the -- returning fire or responding, as you said: When we had to respond, in paragraph 29, to enemy fire at observed positions. And then, of course, as I mentioned, in paragraph 29 you go on to discuss the information that you considered necessary before returning such fire to such locations. And I wanted to ask you if those -- if that particular example reflected in those paragraphs reflects the only circumstances under which you and, insofar as you're aware based on your earlier answer, the corps considered it appropriate to use artillery against targets in depth, that is, use artillery against targets in Sarajevo. Was that it or was there more?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never used artillery in depth, i.e., in Sarajevo, unless our positions were threatened by their mortars and by their artillery from the city. They would skillfully position those in various positions - and that's in my statement, I don't need to go over that again. They were very skilful at positioning their firing positions next to the facilities which were supposed to be protected, i.e., which were not supposed to be targeted, because they knew that if there was no pressing need, we would not open fire on such positions and that was indeed the case. On several occasions while I was the chief of artillery, I sought approval from the brigade commander to open fire on a firing position and that was denied several times; rather, I would be told: Wait, maybe it would die down, order your troops to seek shelter, and that was communicated to our troops. In other words, I was not given approval to open fire on such positions although we suffered quite a number of losses from such fire -- from the fire opened from those positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So you began by directly answering my question but didn't quite complete it because you say you never used artillery in depth, that is, in Sarajevo unless your positions were threatened. And I take it to mean that unless there was -- there had been outgoing fire from those positions or there was outgoing fire from those positions at the time that you considered whether or not to use artillery?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is precisely what I said. We didn't open fire on enemy positions from which they had fired until it was really absolutely necessary to do so, but in that we also bore in mind that we had to reduce the number of civilian casualties to a minimum if we opened fire on such positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So command posts, communications centres, places where -- barracks, places where people assembled, police stations, factories, those kinds of things, those were not targets unless somehow, according to you, fire was launched from that facility?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are all legitimate military targets. They could be targeted, and if there was an ongoing combat those were targeted. Their units that were being assembled, lined up, their command posts, their communication centres because the main goal was to incapacitate the unit for further combat. Their rear units, supply units, their depots, all of those were legitimate military targets that could be targeted. However, we had to have precise information about those targets and we did. We knew that they had been precisely identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, do you consider the fact that something has a military aspect, such as the facilities -- some of the facilities I mentioned before, means that it can be shelled under any circumstances? Once you identify the fact that it has a military aspect, as you say, it becomes a legitimate military target and can be targeted?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have just told you that legitimate military targets in combat, i.e., in mutual engagement, we targeted them because they were legitimate targets and they could be fired upon. I don't see any ambiguities here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What information did you require before targeting, that is, before firing mortars, howitzers, rockets, whatever it was in the particular circumstance against such structures or facilities when there was what you call combat?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received information from the intelligence organ of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps about the deployment of certain elements of the combat order of the enemy forces. We would record that on our maps. We had all the prepared elements for those targets, but we continued observing the sector in order to establish whether the facility was properly described, for example, as a command post. If we could observe the movement of vehicles and troops and if we could monitor through our surveillance means that that was indeed a target that we could fire upon -- so if there was fire, we knew exactly what we were targeting at and where the position in question was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I take it that when you refer to "combat," you're referring to -- you say "mutually engaged." So you're referring to fire coming -- it being exchanged between the VRS and the forces of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And not necessarily from the particular facility that was targeted -- that was ultimately targeted by the SRK?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I did not understand the last portion of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, from your statement, as I mentioned earlier, one could -- well, one I think could only get the impression that the only fire into Sarajevo occurred when there was outgoing fire from a particular position and it was only that particular position when it was -- when it fired, when it was observed, and when your observers provided you with some sort of specific information about it that it was fired upon. But now I understand you to be saying that once there was what you called combat, that all of -- that all kinds of facilities were open for shelling .

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that all the facilities were open for shelling. I mentioned just legitimate targets containing command posts, observation posts, communications centres. Not all the facilities. I'm talking about legitimate targets, legitimate military targets, that's the facilities that I mentioned. I did not have in mind any of the civilian facilities in the town. I did never -- I never said that we could target just any facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm sorry if it sounded like I was mis-characterising your words. I realise that that's not what you were saying a moment ago. My point was that the statement suggests that you would only fire where -- fire at locations where fire had been taken. Now I understand from what you're saying that once fire came from the city that there were -- that other targets that you considered to be legitimate military targets then could be fired -- then could be and were fired upon.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade commander, if we are referring to the period when I was the chief artillery in the brigade, the brigade commander decided on what facilities would be fired upon, i.e., it would be the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps who did that. I opened fire on the observed enemy targets from the positions where the fire had come from, and both commanders had a list and were aware of the deployment of their forces, the deployment of the targets, and they could issue an order to fire upon those legitimate military targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now let me ask you about such orders. Would it be -- when such orders came, did they identify specific military targets, that is, specific buildings or facilities or objects, or did they simply identify a particular area of the city which should be shelled?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First and foremost, it would be the type of target. For example, the brigade command post, the corps command post, the division command post, the observation post of such and such unit, the firing position of that unit, the communications centre of that unit, the type of target was specified in order to select the type of weapons to use. And after that, the part of the city, i.e., the position where that target could be found. I have already told you that we had information about all those targets from before, and if we were told to open fire on the command post of the division, we knew in advance where that command post of that battalion could be located. And that's how we prepared fire and that's how we carried out our firing activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we agree that it would be inappropriate and, indeed, illegal to simply order firing at some general area?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such orders. I don't know if there were any. I never received any such orders, orders to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You appreciate that doesn't quite answer my question; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would consider this to be illegal. Firing upon a city without a specific target, that would be inflicting terror on the civilians, on the population of the city of Sarajevo. I myself never did that. I myself never received an order to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me return for a moment to the precision of the weapons. You had talked about mortars and alluded to the difference in use against potential targets between a mortar with high trajectory and a howitzer. Let me ask you about rockets and multiple-barrel rocket-launchers. Under what circumstances did you consider them to be the most precise weapon for use including potential use in depth?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Multiple-barrel rocket-launchers, for example, are suitable to open fire upon surface targets, targets on the surface. They cover a larger surface of the enemy target. We used multiple-barrel rocket-launchers to open fire on targets mostly during Lukavac 93, on Igman, in front of the forward defence lines of our forces if the position of our weapons were suitable for firing upon such targets, for example, if we were on the flank slope or the forward slope, and this was done because they were very precise and they have an elliptic trajectory and there were no aberrations and their shells were dispersed a little and that's why we chose targets that could be fired upon from such weapons. Those would be targets of -- on the surface, not sheltered. A multiple-barrel rocket-launcher is not intended for destroying facilities; it is intended to destroy manpower in an open area or manpower in trenches which are not covered. I've already told you about mortars. Howitzer also, they could target any target in depth, save for those that were on a rear slope. But it depended on the position of our own weapons and on the position of the enemy trenches, whether they could target targets in front of the forward slope or not. It all depended on the conditions on the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel said: Manpower is being destroyed while attacking our forces, and this was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. That can be checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said in the course of the enemy attack as well as in trenches with light cover or with no cover at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, under what circumstances, if any, would you consider rockets to be an appropriate weapon in -- to be deployed against a densely populated urban area or in the context of a densely populated urban area?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of any such case. I never opened fire on densely populated areas. I don't know of any such cases. I don't know of any cases when multiple-rocket launchers were deployed in a densely populated area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Would that be different for individual rockets as opposed to sending off a salvo of ...?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Individual rockets, guided or semi-guided, 9K11, they could be used against individual targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But not rockets like the 122 Grad or the 128, those would not be appropriate, correct, for use against a densely populated urban area?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't use them, so I don't know, especially I don't know anything about Grad. I had a multiple-rocket launcher in the brigade. I don't know whether fire was opened from the other weapons that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mention in your statement - and you emphasised it again today - that you considered that the ABiH forces used mobile weaponry, such as mobile mortars. Those -- that weaponry I think by definition - as you indicated - is intended to be used and then to move locations as quickly as possible; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And so, first of all, how did you distinguish between a shell that had been fired from a mobile position or a fixed position. And, secondly, did you fire back against mobile weaponry; and if so, for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we observed from our observation posts, we established that they had mobile mortars. They used railway tracks along the railway below the tobacco factory in the direction of Alipasino Polje. There was a railway track over there and on the railway track they positioned mobile mortars. We observed that they opened fire from one position, then they would move the weaponry, and they would fire from a different position. They had firing positions prepared in advance and they had their targets prepared in advance. They needed little time to move their weapons and to take position and open fire. When we established that, if they opened fire from one position, if they fired one or two shells from there, we knew it would move because we knew where it would move to and we were waiting for them to appear there and that's where we opened fire on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the next position where it was expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, I take it your answer was not properly reflected in the transcript. Do you confirm what Mr. Karadzic said? Could you clarify, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. We fired at the following position in the direction of its movement because we had already discovered which position would follow. It wasn't just one, there was several of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What information did you require about the area where the intended fire or the target of the intended fire was to take place? You spoke about observers and requiring particular information. What kind of information was that, apart from the location of the fire you say? What else did you need to know before you would launch a shell or a series of shells? And let me give you a particular example. You spoke in your statement about mortars positioned on buildings. So let's take that as a context, what information did you need?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had organised observation posts at elevated positions around Sarajevo. I have already said in my statement where those posts were located and there were observers who had their areas of observation and they had been trained. For their work they had optical sights, laser devices to measure distance, equipment for observation, laser devices to establish distance, devices to determine the target where it was in relation to the observation post. They had good communications, safe communications, with the unit command, or rather, the brigade command that they were subordinated to. These artillery observers informed about the nature of the target. A mobile mortar, for example, from a certain sector, from roofs as you mentioned, these observers observed the positions throughout the day, they were at the post continually, they had shifts, and they would easily observe any changes in their areas of observation. They would notice if a building had been hit when they saw a flash, for example, and then suddenly they would see that something was missing. They would observe that location and then they noticed that the tiles were being removed from the roofs, that you could just put a barrel through a hole so that it could be fired and then you would see a flash and then the hole would be closed as soon as it had fired. And that is how we established that we were dealing with a mortar position. As to whether the house was inhabited or not, whether there was anyone there or not, well, they were responsible for the fact that they didn't take into account where they placed their firing positions. I and my subordinates never allowed civilians to walk around firing positions, and especially not children. Boys, 13, 14 years old are curious, they want to see weapons, but we did not allow children to approach firing positions. In case of enemy action, we didn't want any civilian casualties. And they had to take care of their own civilians, as far as I'm concerned. This was a matter of directly putting civilians at risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What about the use of artillery, that is, the use of shelling, intended to punish the population of Sarajevo for the fact that firing had taken place from within Sarajevo? Was that a lawful or appropriate military tactic?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never had the intention of firing on civilians or punishing civilians in Sarajevo. We always took care to protect civilians, to avoid civilian casualties, and to avoid destroying civilian buildings. We never wanted to do such things in the course of shelling. As I have already said, I think that firing positions were deliberately established by the Muslim army in the vicinity of facilities that should have been protected. They thought that in this way they were protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you said that in your statement before, Colonel. I wanted to know if it was illegal to use shelling against Sarajevo in order to send a punitive message that the -- that any further military manoeuvres or outgoing fire should not take place?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received such orders and I'm not aware of any such orders having been issued in order to punish the civilians, in order to open fire on facilities in the town without there being any need to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you never heard of the use of massively disproportionate fire back into Sarajevo - and by that I mean two or three outgoing shells and dozens and dozens and dozens of incoming shells from the VRS into Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard about such cases. I didn't do such things because we didn't even have enough ammunition. We had to save ammunition because in the second part of the war, the Muslim forces had far more ammunition and they fired on Serbian positions far more than the Serbian artillery on their positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you about a couple of other matters. We recently heard evidence from a former member of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade who explained to the Trial Chamber, among other things, about a road that was held within VRS-controlled territory but which was "constantly under fire" and therefore "under control of the BH army." That can be found at transcript pages 29189 through 90. Am I correct that this tactic, that is, keeping a road under -- constantly under fire, is something that's referred to generally as fire control and were you familiar with that approach to the use of artillery by either of the ABiH or the VRS?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if you're referring to the Hresa-Vogosca road. It's the only road and link to the south and south-western [as interpreted] part of Sarajevo, Serbian Sarajevo at the time. I know that that road was under sniper fire from the Muslim forces in several areas and also it -- mortars fired on it. There were casualties. It was difficult to use that road to get to Vogosca, Ilijas, Ilidza, and so on and so forth. The Muslim forces frequently fired on that road.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a comment on the transcript. The witness said "north-west" not "south-west."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, probably it's about the Hresa or Hresa-Vogosca road is the only part linking to the south and south-western part of Sarajevo. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] North-west, north and north-west.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I didn't direct your attention to the use of fire control on any particular road. I'm just asking if you're familiar with the concept generally?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And am I correct that that's something that would be appropriate or lawful in the context of a road that was -- a communication road that was outside the city and controlled by the opposite side's forces but would not be lawful in the context of a road in a densely populated urban area?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It wouldn't be correct to fire on a densely inhabited area. All the streets, all the roads, are used by the inhabitants, by civilians, so it wouldn't be lawful to fire on the civilians, to fire on those streets; and we didn't act in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, for planning purposes, the Chamber has been requested to take a break at 10.15, that is now, for some technical reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. President. Thank you for letting me know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, before we continue, may I just please introduce Mr. Alex Friede, who has been working with my team now since August of this year and has been an invaluable member of the team. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Tieger, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, this Trial Chamber has received extensive evidence from UNPROFOR personnel, military observers, international negotiators, journalists, various citizens, and others that, contrary to what you've told us about the practices of the VRS in connection with the shelling of Sarajevo, that the Bosnian Serb military forces engaged for months and years in the specific shelling of civilian areas, the random shelling of the town including civilian areas, random shelling not intended for any specific point target, and the existence of punitive shelling by pounding the area. Now, against that backdrop, I wanted to inform you that I want to take you to certain documentation, contemporaneous documentation, reflecting what was happening at the time. First of all, we discussed the issue of punitive firing earlier and you provided an answer about that. So in connection with that, I'd like to turn to P01041.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're doing that, I want to object to the comment that Mr. Tieger made in which he purported to inform the witness about testimony that's been given at this trial. Since it was not accompanied by a question, I think it is the kind of improper type of comment that you frequently chastised Dr. Karadzic for.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask a question in that case. I just wanted to move on, but that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, were you aware of the fact that internationals within Sarajevo present day after day after day were observing what they considered to be punitive fire, disproportionate fire, firing at civilian areas, and a random fire not intended at any point target? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, in my statement I said that UNPROFOR officers at the artillery positions of the brigade group -- well, they were there from the end of June 1992 up until the end of the war. They were on duty day and night at the command position of the mixed artillery battalion and they were accompanied by an interpreter. At the same time, these UNPROFOR were aware of the following. If it was necessary to retaliate, to open fire, to fire in the depth of the enemy territory, they were informed of the type of the target concerned, of the position from which artillery was firing on the target, and they were also informed on the number of shells fired on the target. And they then sent reports to their superiors, to the command, to the superior central - I don't know how to call it - and if they reported objectively, and I don't doubt that that was the case -- well, they were immediately informed of all cases of fire being opened and of what was done. So there's nothing that can be concealed. They immediately submitted reports after action had been taken. They asked for co-ordinates for the firing positions. They heard about this two days later, they found out about all the positions, and from that command position they could see from which positions fire was being opened, they listed the weapons, everything was under UNPROFOR control. They had co-ordinates on the targets and information on the nature of the target. As to whether they reported on action against our position, not only our firing positions but the positions of our units, if they were providing support, well, I don't know about that. Perhaps there was some other team that was responsible for such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So do I understand you correctly that it's your position that when UNPROFOR or other UN officials complained, as they did repeatedly, to VRS officials about the firing on civilians or civilian neighbourhoods or civilian objects, that they were in a position to know exactly what they were talking about?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what sort of complained they filed with the VRS command. I do know that they were informed on our artillery action because all the artillery positions around Sarajevo are checked by them. They were at some positions day and night and others were visited. They knew where our positions were, they could hear where action was being taken from, and they could visit the positions and check things. But at the artillery positions of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade, the brigade artillery, they were present there 24 hours a day with an interpreter. And they were immediately informed of any fire being opened on the unit being -- on the unit opening fire on the target being fired on and on the reasons for which this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You said you didn't know what complaints they made. Does that mean that there was no occasion on which your corps commanders notified his personnel that there had been specific complaints by UN officials about the shelling of civilian areas and demand to know what was going on?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that a request was made for a report from the superior command after the Vase Miskina case, after Markale I, after Markale II, and so on and so forth. This concerned about whether a unit took action and which unit, so the dates of these events are known. UNPROFOR had to make a note of the positions from which fire was opened, if fire was opened from certain positions. So I'm familiar with certain incidents that occurred in town and the superior command requested a report from subordinate units, a report on whether fire had been opened from certain artillery positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, a few moments ago, at page 28, you said there's nothing that can be concealed. Isn't it a fact, Colonel, that a concealment and deception of UNPROFOR and the internationals was undertaken repeatedly by the SRK to mask their intentions, to hide their weapons, and generally to be able to do what they wanted to do despite the presence of the international community?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said nothing was concealed, well, at those positions even if you wanted to hide certain things, it wasn't possible. If you fire an artillery shell from a howitzer, from a gun, if you fire a shell from a mortar, this cannot be concealed. It's not a rifle bullet that doesn't allow you to determine where it was fired from. So if they were on duty in the immediate vicinity of those firing positions or at the command post of the battalion, they were immediately aware of what was going on. We can't say we didn't open fire if the firing position is 200 metres away. So how shall I put it? That would have been crazy. It wasn't our intention to conceal anything. We immediately informed them of everything. Even if we had wanted to, we wouldn't have been able to conceal anything, but I'm not saying that the corps command wanted to conceal anything and to deceive UNPROFOR. It wasn't possible to do that and we didn't have such an intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn to P1670, please. This reflects an order dated the 21st of August, 1994, from General Milosevic. And let's turn to the second page in the English. And that refers to an order for the immediate removal of anti-aircraft guns and relocation to new firing positions where they will be camouflaged and sheltered. In item 4 [sic], order that all the heavy weapons in the 20-kilometre zone around Sarajevo be camouflaged and hidden. Move weapons through the 20-kilometre zone only in accordance with the orders so that if the need arises for such movements, they would be concealed from UNPROFOR forces. Turn also in that connection to P00847, which reflects a February very urgent order, February 9th, 1994, to be precise, from the Main Staff, specifically from deputy commander General Milovanovic, ordering the movement of artillery, mainly inoperative weapons, from certain positions and indicating that the commanders of the corps shall put the inoperative weapons unconditionally at the disposal of, and then there's an illegible commander, in order to disguise our intentions. And then if the cease-fire agreement is signed, these inoperative artillery pieces could then be removed while the current basic weapons could remain for use. And finally if we could turn quickly to D00312. Page 7 of the English, please, and it's item 5 of the B/C/S which will be at approximately -- you see the -- keep scrolling through the B/C/S, please. There it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be zoomed in? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could go to the next page of the B/C/S. Right, and it's toward the bottom of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is an analysis of combat-readiness. This was tendered by the Defence. And at this particular part of the analysis it indicates that: "UNPROFOR observers and units have been stationed near our positions; they have been observed closely in order to prevent them to come to our positions and collect intelligence data." Colonel, contrary to your suggestion that there was never any intention on the part of the command to deceive UNPROFOR or the UNMOs in any way, there was a willingness, interest, and effort to do so; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, about the first document, that document refers to anti-aircraft defence weapons. It would be the chief of the anti-aircraft defence in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps that is -- was in charge of that. At that time I was the commander of the mixed anti-artillery regiment and my weapons were on positions also under the control of UNPROFOR and they were inactive. So I wouldn't be able to say anything about the first document. As for the last paragraph in the last document under number 5, as far as I understand it says that in the course of the war, not a single unit of ours has been taken by surprise by the infiltrated enemy DTGs, and I believe that this concerns the DTGs. This doesn't concern UNPROFOR. The intention is to prevent DTGs to come in contact with our troops. This does not apply to UNPROFOR. It does not apply to preventing UNPROFOR from coming to our positions. I think this is the way to understand it. I'm not familiar with any order. No order arrived at my position to conceal my artillery. When I was in charge of artillery during the periods that I mentioned in the statement, all that artillery was under control of UNPROFOR forces from day one to the last day. There are reports to that effect which can easily be verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me make sure I understand you clearly, Colonel, do I understand you, then, that your position is that you didn't hide your weaponry but you're not in a position to know what others did?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I did not need conceal anything. What I had was on display. At the beginning of the war, when UNPROFOR arrived in June 1992, we displayed everything to them, they made a record of everything, and the weapons could not be moved from those positions. When we did move them, the UNPROFOR knew from what position to what position, they knew and they immediately established that those were the weapons that they were aware of. They had the serial numbers and they could check them at any moment. Those were not rifles that you can put on your shoulder and move them as you wished. Those were heavy artillery weapons and UNPROFOR inspected our positions and our weapons every day.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down when answering questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, I don't know if you received this in B/C/S, but you have been asked to slow your rate of speech down so the interpreters can keep up.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What the witness said has not been recorded. They could also see whether the weapons had been approached or not. The witness said that and it was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Approached by who, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The crews. If fire had to be opened, crews would approach those weapons and the UNPROFOR knew about that, they were informed about that, and they could observe that themselves. Howitzers were not moved every day from one position to the next. We did change firing positions from time to time, and UNPROFOR was made aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, let's return to where we were before we discussed briefly the issue of concealment and that was the issue of the contemporaneous documentation bearing on the question of the nature of the artillery fire against Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I had just asked before we moved to the issue we just discussed to call up P01041 and I'd ask that that be called to the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be zoomed in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is an intercepted telephone discussion involving General Mladic on the 25th of May, 1992, and General Mladic says: "If a single bullet is fired at you or at 'Jusuf Dzonlic' barracks or at 'Marsal Tito' barracks, or if a single soldier is wounded, either at the front or in the barracks, I will retaliate against the town." And he goes on to note that "Sarajevo is going to shake." And, Colonel, I put it to you that contrary to your suggestion that there was no punitive fire or at least that you claim not to have been aware of it, that from the outset of the war, at this very -- from the very early stage of the war, that was a feature of the shelling of Sarajevo by the Bosnian Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I still claim -- I was a battery commander at this time when this document was drafted. I never communicated with General Mladic; I was not in a position to do so. So I don't know whether he ordered any such thing. I cannot say anything about this document. No order from anybody arrived at my address to retaliate against the city and to punish civilians. So my firing positions were never involved in any such thing. No such thing was ever done from my firing positions. Maybe General Mladic did say that in order to avert the attention of the other side, to warn them, to make them stop firing at our positions. At that time in June, a major enemy offensive was launched from the city. Maybe that's why this order was issued. I can only speculate what General thought when he said that because no such order ever reached me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, there are a number of ways possibly of being aware of whether or not this position articulated by General Mladic on the 25th of May came to fruition or not. So let me show you a couple of film clips to see whether or not that happened, and then I'm going to ask you how it was that you weren't aware of whether or not General Mladic's threat that Sarajevo would shake came to pass or not. So if we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would it be fair on the witness to show him the entire document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's for you to take up that issue later on in your re-examination. Let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And I'd like to look at P931 and P932 , please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Every night in Sarajevo you think it can't get worse, but it does, making a mockery of the attempts of mediators to bring peace to the city which is enfolded in war" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, shall we stop here. Now I note that the B/C/S translation has started. Let's continue -- or shall we begin again? I think that's fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "Every night in Sarajevo you think it can't get worse, but it does, making a mockery of the attempts of mediators to bring peace to this city which is enfolded in war. "Less than 24 hours earlier, the Serb commanders had put their signatures on yet another agreement affirming a truce never adhered to and their readiness to re-open the airport. Now the Serb gunners in the hills show where their true commitment lies. Under a sickle moon, the city rocks to the explosions. "Lit up by fire and the mass of glowing sparks adrift across its roofs" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we stop again? I don't think -- did you hear the translation, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not a single word of the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May it be noted that the interpreters have not been provided with the transcript of the video-clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it was translated into French but not into B/C/S. I'll leave it to you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I confirm with the B/C/S booth whether it was impossible to translate without the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The B/C/S booth confirms this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll try to proceed without it. We can get -- meanwhile maybe we can -- in case its turns out to be necessary on the responses, we'll move to get it to the translators if we can do that within two minutes. Meanwhile I think I can proceed without it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Witness, you saw the images. This is a broadcast of the 7th of June, 1992, and it refers to the firing of shells from Serb gunners in the hills and that this night-time firing indicates that a mass of glowing sparks, sparks drifting across roof-tops, et cetera. And I don't know whether or not you could actually hear the shells being fired, but I presume you could. Let me try to move on to a shelling that took place on the 9th of June, two days later, and that's P932.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "No district spared. "All shaking as every ten seconds the rocket shells and mortars land. The fire so heavy, so incessant, that the deadly streams of light crisscross each other."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us stop here again. If this is not translated, it's fair to play it without sound because the English transcription is transcribed in the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I think we need the sound for the sounds of the shells, if no other reason, and I'm -- if necessary, I'll wait the minute or two to get to the booths so this can be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we come to this issue later on because the transcription could be provided to the booth very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to return to that video momentarily, Colonel. Meanwhile, I want to bring your attention to a couple of other issues, and that's the issue of -- of specific targets versus shelling areas and scattering shots around the city. So in that connection I'd like to turn to P0518.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The B/C/S booth has now received the transcript of the second video. Could the same courtesy be extended to the French booth, i.e., they need a transcript as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, P0 -- I'm sorry, P01518, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, this is General Mladic, this time on the 28th of May, now discussing where to fire of the artillery into Sarajevo with Mirko Vukasinovic. And as you see, General Mladic tells him: "Shoot at Velesici, also at Pofalici, there's not much Serb population there." And then tells him: "Shoot there, around Dobrovoljacka Street, up around Humska," and they talk about Djure Djakovica Street. And then General Mladic explains: "Apply artillery" -- it's translated as "reconnaissance" here, the word may be closer to "observation" or "monitoring," "so that they cannot sleep, that we roll out of their minds ..." All right I'm going to show you two more quickly along the same lines. Next 1511. General Mladic again, this time on the 29th, this time speaking to Mr. Potpara. And he says: "As soon as the motherfuckers attack you, fire at them. Can you hit the railway station?" He says: "Hit them with something and scatter them around." And finally P1521. If we can turn the second page of the English and the second page of the B/C/S. General Mladic again, again with Vukasinovic, telling him to fire at Velesici and then asking: "Can you also shell Bascarsija?" And when he receives an affirmative answer from Vukasinovic saying: "Fire a salvo at Bascarsija as well." Now, Colonel, I've just shown you three reflections of the kind of shelling and targeting that was going on. First of all, it's true, isn't it, that those documents reflect the shelling of areas and not point targeting ordered by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I just told you a little while ago, according to what I know, I did not receive any such orders. You see who this applied to, you see what firing positions this applies to. They were never under my control, I was never in command of those, I never received any such orders. If there are documents to that effect, I suppose that such orders were issued; however, you can see from Colonel Vukasinovic's answers, we responded, i.e., they returned fire. They fired upon the firing positions from which they had been fired at. That was the end of May and the beginning of June. This was a major offensive by the enemy troops, and I just heard on the clip the cannonade of shells but there was nothing less happening in Lukavica, so it was an exchange of fire on both sides. I'm sure that civilians did get hurt, that civilian facilities did get destroyed, but the culprits should be sought on the other side. According to what I know, it was not our intention to fire -- to shell the city just for the firing sake. Velesici is mentioned here. You shouldn't forget that the Serbian population from Velesici had been expelled and slaughtered. Only small groups managed to break through, and I believe that the audio was to the effect of firing at Velesici because of that, because that population had experienced an exodus in the months of May and June. They had to flee from the territory of Velesici. And here they mentioned targets, the railway station. And from the sector of the railway station not only mortars fired but also tanks and cannons, weapons of a longer range. So the target was not a railway station -- the railway station but a military target in the vicinity of the railway station. This means that those were responses to the enemy offensive that was launched at the time. Fire was opened in order to protect the Serbian population that was pulling out from Zuc, Velesici, and Hum, and other sectors. And I underline once again, according to what I know, and you have to bear in mind that I never received such orders, you can see which units this applied to, and you know what units I was responsible for and you can conclude whether I was in a position to know about this. As for the firing and the cannonade of shells, this was just our response. And now you actually brought me down the memory lane. And now I remember everything that I had to go through in 1992, all the terror, all those horrific things that I experienced.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in that connection then let me return to P932 for which there is now a transcript in the booth --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that because -- Mr. Simic you tried to explain General Mladic's position. I'm asking this. Shall I upload P1511, the previous intercept where Mladic was indicating to hit the railway station, and you explained to us the reason why Mladic was ordering to hit a railway station. But after that he -- Mladic said - could you zoom in a bit further - "Hit them with something" and he continued saying "and scatter them around." What does it mean, "scattering them around"? Why did he need to scatter the shells around? Could you explain that as well, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what he had in mind, but I think that they are thinking about the target that they're firing on in the vicinity of the railway station. First he didn't say "destroy," destroy, disperse them so that they stop acting from that sector. I don't know what General Mladic had in mind, but in my opinion, that is what it would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Tieger, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, I had asked to play P932 in response to your suggestion that you didn't know whether Mladic's threat that the town would shake had transpired or not. So let me play that again for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "No district spared. "All shaking as every ten seconds the rocket shells and mortars land, the fire so heavy, so incessant that the deadly streams of light crisscross each other. By early Monday morning, the inundation of the hospitals begins. For the doctors and the nurses of the city's former military hospital, already up throughout the night, the beginning of a dark, grim day, the like of which they've never known. Trained fingers which for 24 hours will work without respite, to stem blood, extract jagged metal, preserve life. But so many casualties of" --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, you had a chance to see both 931 and 932, the shelling that took place both on the 7th or the broadcast that took place reflecting the shellings that took place. Those broadcasts were on the 7th and the 9th. I suggest to you that you would have been well aware of the fact that General Mladic's threat to make the town shake had, indeed, occurred .

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, as far as I can see from this clip, the first person wounded who was shown here, 30 or 40 years old, wasn't a civilian. I think he had a military boot on his foot, so he was a military target and he was wounded. This happens, one is wounded or killed in war. Unfortunately, there were civilian casualties too. I think the second image showed a boy. Unfortunately, these such things happened too because it's an urban settlement, an inhabited settlement. I won't forget the cannonade of the Muslim artillery in May 1992. I'll repeat that, their intention was to breakthrough the city as soon as possible and to take up positions around the town. That was their intention, their objective, at the time. Hundreds, thousands, of shells hit the surrounding villages. We also sustained casualties at our positions and in particular in villages, in settlements where there were no firing positions, but they fired at random on those targets. So there was fire in retaliation and there were probably civilian casualties. That's what I can say about this. I do remember the period of May and June. And if I could just add another sentence, I know that during that period I couldn't sleep for two nights, for example. In the course of the day I tried to find half an hour to have a bit of a rest because they were continually requesting support for the forces at the front line not to target the town because these forces hadn't fortified themselves correctly and hadn't secured the line. So it was necessary to maintain the positions that had been taken at the very beginning, and they were maintained until the end of the war and perhaps there were very minor movements forward or backwards. It doesn't mean that they were at rest, that they were inactive, and that we targeted them; that is not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You referred to thousands of shells from Muslim artillery. Are you suggesting to this Court, Colonel, that there was basically parity in the amount of weaponry, amount and nature of weaponry, between the ABiH and the VRS at this time and that the shelling by the ABiH was equivalent to or greater than the incoming fire to Sarajevo by the VRS? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already told you, at the beginning we had more equipment but they soon consolidated themselves and obtained ammunition and weapons. The Viktor Bubanj barracks, the Marsal Tito barracks, Jusuf Dzonlic were abandoned, all of these were abandoned. A column in Dobrovoljacka was cut off in army command. Weapons were taken away. In the Marsal Tito barracks quite a few artillery pieces remained and the school -- moved it from Zadar to the Marsal Tito barracks, 115-millimetre howitzers remained there, tanks, 122-millimetre howitzers, Gvozdiks, personnel carriers and mortars -- a number of mortars remained there. So it's not as if they were unarmed. From the very beginning they fired on us from tanks and cannons and this gradually grew more and more intensive. There were flame-launchers and perhaps an Oganj, but I'm not sure. All of these things were in the Marsal Tito barracks. They remained in the Marsal Tito barracks when the JNA left the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn to P2668 and see how General Milosevic characterised it in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't say Gvozdik or multiple-rocket launcher or flame-launcher, perhaps. Oganj is also not included in the transcript so the transcript is not quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me just point out these kinds of interventions for the transcript I know are not going to -- I think we're all accustomed to the fact when the speaker is moving quickly, the transcript doesn't always immediately reflect those remarks and that's, as I understand it, remedied through a process after court. But I'm at the Court's disposal for that. I just don't know how many interruptions are useful when we have a speaker who is going on for a long period of time in a fast manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I -- I note there are several phonetic marks, so I take it that that will be taken care of by the court reporters. Do you confirm, Mr. Simic, having said those things referred to by Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I said multiple-rocket launcher, flame-thrower, I'm not sure about the Oganj. I also mentioned the Gvozdik and the howitzers, the 122 -- the D-30 as well. I didn't say the D-30 but I had that in mind, too. They're the Gvozdiks that are 120-millimetre -- that have 122-millimetre calibre as well. So I mentioned all of these items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again, given that everything you say is to be translated, please slow down in answering the question, Mr. Simic. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, I told you we wanted to look at a warning issued by General Milosevic in July of 1995 to the brigades, and if you look at the beginning of paragraph 4, we see that General Milosevic says: "While we used massive artillery at a time when the enemy had just a few mortars and the occasional gun, we did not manage to settle the war ..." That's a reference to the period in 1992, including the period we've just been looking at, Colonel, isn't it, and a reflection of the fact that there was a dramatically disproportionate array of weaponry at the disposal of the two forces?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not disputing the fact that it was disproportionate at the beginning of the war. I said this on two or three occasions. At the beginning of the war that was the case, but gradually they armed themselves in various ways. Certain witnesses will testify about this after me, witnesses who are familiar with how they obtained weapons and ammunition. I only heard about this and wouldn't want to go into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Who are those witnesses, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I say there will probably be witnesses from those areas who will be called here, that will probably be the case, perhaps brigade commanders who controlled the passage of convoys of alleged humanitarian aid, of what was supposed to be humanitarian aid. But amongst the humanitarian aid they would find ammunition and weapons and so on and so forth in their areas of responsibility. I heard about that, there was such cases -- I only heard about it so I can't confirm this, but there will probably be someone who personally experienced this. I don't know who these witnesses will be, but I assume that they will include brigade commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at some of the other things that General Milosevic had to say to the troops in 1995.
