He notes in the first paragraph that for the first time, for the first time, we are faced with the fact that on top of having the advantage in manpower, now the enemy has an advantage of artillery. And then he goes on in the second paragraph to note the following: "Despite being aware that we are facing problems in ammunition production, especially of specific types, we are continuing with this lax behaviour and are spending ammunition as if we had it in abundance, trying at any cost to outfire the enemy artillery. That is why we very often fire at inhabited settlements and specific buildings when there are no combat actions whatsoever, spending vast quantities of ammunition, without paying attention to the fact that we will not have anything to stop the enemy when it comes to mounting a decisive defence." And then he goes on in the third paragraph to note roughly -- essentially the same thing, expressing that it is inexplicable that some brigades are spending much more ammunition firing at inhabited settlements where there is no combat than others who are repelling fierce attacks. Now, contrary to your suggestion earlier, I think at page 24, that there wasn't the massive use of artillery against Sarajevo by the VRS because of a lack of ammunition, General Milosevic confirms precisely the opposite, that the SRK was expending vast amounts of artillery and doing so against inhabited settlements where there were no combat actions. That's the reality, isn't it, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, all artillery units had to face up to this lack of ammunition. They tried to save ammunition. In 1995 I was an official in the artillery organ and I visited the positions. I gathered information with regard to the amount of ammunition available and I conveyed orders from the chief of artillery and from Commander Milosevic according to which ammunition should be saved. Only well-observed targets should be fired on if fire could be adjusted. This was in order to save ammunition and to be as effective as possible. There are probably cases, as stated in this document, where certain troops spent more ammunition than necessary and they probably targeted targets that they shouldn't have. I can't say whether this was the case or not, but the general did issue warnings and said that it was necessary to save ammunition, to use ammunition sparingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I had asked you earlier about both offensive operations and I wanted to turn quickly to P5940. This refers to the Talis 2 operation in 1995, and again, Colonel, this would appear to be an offensive operation, indicating that the VRS forces shall continue fighting further to the Main Staff directive with the objective of seizing the Lukavac village-Siljak-Mocevici village line. So would this be another offensive operation?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This isn't an offensive operation. It's an offensive action, the purpose of which is to improve the tactical position in Lukavica and Siljak sector and so on and so forth. That is where the Muslim forces moved our positions back in the direction of Trnovo and this order in particular concerns improving the tactical position in the Zlatiste sector, the Debelo Brdo and Brajkovac sector, so that's to the south or south-east of Sarajevo, roughly speaking. So it concerned improving the tactical position, moving the line by a hundred or 200 metres, even less in certain areas, perhaps 50 metres in certain areas. So that order concerned the 9th of May, 1995. It's not a matter of operation. That would include all the brigade -- all the corps brigades which would have different tasks. Here it says improve the position, take back positions at Siljak, Proskok and so on and so forth, and take Debelo Brdo, Brajkovac, Rajlaca [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The order also refers to placing a major part of Stari Grad under fire control with the objective of ultimate victory. Now, I asked you questions about fire control earlier and you indicated that it would not be lawful or appropriate in the context of an urban area.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand it, you said that most of Stari Grad should be placed under fire control. In order to control their fire, it was necessary to improve the tactical position of our forces so that we could control their fire coming from the inside because that part of town on Zlatiste was a road that was targeted by snipers and mortars from their positions. This was continually the case. In order to establish control over that road and control the fire they opened from the inside -- well, I think that's what we had in mind not to establish fire control. We can establish fire control, or rather, we can control matters. It doesn't mean we will fire. To have control and to open fire doesn't mean the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you can have fire control without fire? Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can have control. In order to prevent them from taking action, we can have control over the town. We can observe it without taking action, without firing on the town if fire isn't opened from the other side. Since we knew where our positions were and a breakthrough couldn't be achieved, they wouldn't try to do anything if they didn't believe that they could be successful in their attempt, if they didn't believe they could attain their objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, how are you going to convey the message that they can't be successful in their objective if there is a moratorium on any fire in order to achieve fire control?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the ban on opening fire, the Serbian forces never or almost never broke the truce. They weren't the first to do that. This was always done by the other side in order to provoke the units of the VRS, to provoke them to react, and they did this deliberately. This was the case from the very beginning of the war. Even if there were negotiations on moving the artillery at the time, if there was anything that was to their benefit --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, no, Colonel, stop -- please --

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I apologise for that, but I'm asking you about this particular order and this particular effort toward the objective of achieving ultimate victory. And I'm not going to ask you another rhetorical question. I'm going to put it to you more directly that this was an order to achieve control over Stari Grad through the use of artillery fire in the same manner as the fire-control discussion we had before about keeping a road under fire control by firing at it constantly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see item 4 in the English version --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Wait, wait, wait --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- item 4 that the Prosecution is referring to now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you referring to para 4, Mr. Tieger, or number 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's also in -- I directed the witness's attention to para 2. It's also in para 4 with the same language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, then it's fair to show para 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's here now but not in English. Do you remember the question or shall I ask Mr. Tieger to repeat his question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, paragraph 2 and paragraph 4 show quite clearly what Mr. -- what General Milosevic said. Mount a decisive defence of the positions obtained and improve tactical positions and breakthrough to certain elevations above Sarajevo in order to establish control over Sarajevo, the Stari Grad that you're talking about, in order to gain control and to have a better view of that part of the town. That's what he has in mind. He doesn't mean establish artillery control. To control and to open fire is not the same thing. In paragraph 4 it says: I have decided to use the main units of the corps to mount a decisive offence of the positions and to breakthrough to Debelo Brdo and Grdonj. These are hills above Sarajevo. It's not in the town; it's above the town. One of the places is near Lukavica-Zlatiste-Pale road and the other near Hresa-Vogosca road. So it was necessary to establish control of those hills that were making it difficult to use those roads. That's what it says quite clearly in paragraph 2 and paragraph 4 in this decision from the corps commander. I don't understand what is not clear here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So your -- Colonel, your testimony is that the -- that establishing -- the language establishing fire control is not a reference to artillery use but instead a reference to the physical control of roads above Stari Grad?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says achieve control of the Stari Grad, achieve firing control. It doesn't say the artillery. It says we should be able to control that part, that the road is practicable. We need to control that part. It doesn't say fire on the Stari Grad from artillery and infantry weapons. It says place under control, it means establish control over the situation and have an advantageous position, which would be the case if we took those elevations. So it was an offensive action, not an operation, because it was in a small part of the front. That's where the action was taken. It has nothing to do with an attack launched on Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I just suggest something. In the document it says "shallow," but the transcript never uses this term. The Colonel often mentions shallow incursions. It's not a breakthrough, it's an incursion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's again a subject for you to take up in your re-examination. I think we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, in fact, Colonel, the person responsible for fire control of Stari Grad -- well, first of all, let me -- there were no military targets in Stari Grad that you named in your statement, were there?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, from the very beginning of the war, from Bistrik and from the other side of Sedrenik and from that sector, mortar fire was opened on Serbian positions in Miljevici, Lukavica, Grbavica, as well as Mrkovici and Kresa and so on and so forth. In other words, I remember that there were such things. At the end of the war, in 1995, they provided support to their forces from those areas; in other words, there was mortar fire opened from Stari Grad, from that part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm referring in particular to paragraph 23 of your statement. And as it happens, Colonel, the person responsible for placing a major part of Stari Grad under fire control was the deputy chief of artillery, you; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not be responsible for placing Stari Grad under control. I could not be the deputy chief of artillery. I was a desk officer in artillery. It must have been somebody above me. When it comes specifically to this operation on Debelo Brdo, Rajkovac, I was responsible. Probably the chief of artillery was absent. So I was not responsible for placing Stari Grad under control but on that particular axis, Zlatiste-Kula and an elevation which is specified in the order, on that axis - I could show you that on a map if you have one - in the Rajkovac sector I was responsible for that. I was not responsible for placing Stari Grad under control. It doesn't specify so in the order nor was I responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, because of the time I want to move on to the issue of air bombs which you address in paragraphs 21 through 22 of your statement. And in that statement you appear to be a proponent of the precision and accuracy of air bombs, emphasising that the weapons were very precise, just like standard artillery weapons. In terms of direction, there was almost no deviation in relation to the recorded elements. First of all, I wanted to ask you what you -- what your experience was with air bombs. You note in your statement that you personally observed the effects of a modified air bomb twice. That's in paragraph 22. Apart from those instances, what other experience or responsibilities did you have in connection with air bombs?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, what I stated under 21, I would like to repeat that the first time I encountered an air bomb was in the second half of 1994. That was the first time I came across modified air bombs and air launchers. That was the first time I observed their activity on the forward line of the enemy in Nisici plateau. Based on that experience and based on my second experience in the Trnovo sector, I don't know when that was, I believe that it was either in November or December, before the final cease-fire was agreed, that was the command post of the 81st Infantry Battalion of the Muslim forces. And based on those two instances about the behaviour of the weapons during fire, they hit the target that I requested, I saw the weapons at the time which could not be made by laymen but by professionals. They possessed everything else that the other classic artillery weapons had, optical sights, mechanisms for moving the launcher in height, and that also required trained crew and that's how targets were hit. I don't know whether there were any other experiences. I don't know. I shared with you my experience, my personal experience, and what I saw and I claim that with full responsibility. I don't know if there were any other different experiences in other areas; I wouldn't be able to tell you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, Colonel, the question was: Apart from seeing air bombs used twice, did you have anything else to do with them? And then you proceeded to tell me again, as is contained in your statement, that you saw them twice and then you repeated most of what is contained in paragraphs 21 through 22. My question was: Apart from that, did you have anything to do with air bombs?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no. I was not in charge, I was not involved, nor was I able to be involved in any shape or form with that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And let's be clear about what we're talking about when we're talking about air bombs, though I think some aspects of your statement make clear. In paragraph 22 you identify the reason why you think air bombs came into use and that was because the VRS had them in stock. It wasn't possible to use them in the conventional way by dropping them from airplanes. And it was a handy way to compensate for some of the -- of what you referred to as the classical artillery ammunition the VRS lacked. So what we're talking about here is basically this, that you're talking about bombs that are intended to be dropped from airplanes; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With huge explosive potential?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: VRS is unable to deliver them with airplanes and so it devised a way to deliver them in another manner and that was by using rockets to propel them?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, rocket engines from a launch pad. That's how they were launched and that's how they were able to hit targets, something to that effect, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: How were the rockets affixed to the air bombs in order to get them to the -- to get them to wherever the alleged target was?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a rocket -- an air bomb became a rocket. It was rendered capable of becoming a rocket. A rocket engine was attached to the back of the air bomb, there was a stabiliser attached to that, and a certain quantity of rocket gunpowder which was activated by electricity. An air bomb, when it became a rocket, was attached -- it was affixed to a launch pad. There was a device that held it to the launch pad. When it was activated, the fuel was activated, and that's what propelled the air bomb which became a rocket because it had rocket propellant and that's how it could fly all the way to the target. If you had all the tables where the professionals had calculated how far the rocket would fly and with which quantity of fuel, that's the elements that we took into account, the length. And there is also the classical targeting because there were devices for moving the launcher in height and precision tools for targeting. So there was no difference in sights or setting up targets, but just the fuel. The air bomb would become a rocket if provided with --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, interpreters noted that you are speaking too fast. Could you repeat from the part when you referred to: "... air bomb would become a rocket if provided with ..." from there. After you said: "There is no difference in sights or setting up targets, but just the fuel," could you repeat from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Prosecutor asked me how that rocket was affixed to the air bomb. It was not that the rocket was attached to the air bomb, but in factual terms the air bomb became a rocket when a rocket engine was attached to the rear of that bomb and it had rocket charge and that changed its purpose and it was no longer an air bomb but a rocket. That's what we can call it. Although we did not call it a rocket because it was launched in a similar way as any other rockets in multiple-rocket launchers called Plamen and Oganj.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Let's take a look at 65 ter 40099.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The detachment devised and in practice proved the application of utility in sabotage uses. The 21st Detachment for the first time used the mobile rocket-launcher." May it be noted that the interpreters were not provided with a transcript of this video. "An exceptional fire-power of the detachment reflected in the ability to launch 18 shells and 152, 57-millimetre rockets."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Colonel, is that one of the ways in which air bombs became -- as you put it, became rockets?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That would be the way. However, I never saw such a launcher with five launching pads. I never saw that. I saw just the one with the one launch pad. I suppose that the sabotage detachment of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had that, but I never saw it. This is about 57-millimetre rocket-launcher. I'm not familiar with this weapon, but that's how it was done. A rocket engine was affixed to the air bomb and that's how an air bomb became a rocket, if we're talking about air bombs. I believe that my explanation, the way I provided it, is very much reflected in the video-clip that we have just seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In addition to screwing a rocket into the back end of an air bomb, were rockets also affixed to air bombs -- to larger air bombs by welding them -- welding a number of rockets, that is, three or four, to the body of the air bomb and launching it in that fashion?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. It's a technical issue how things were affixed to each other. Maybe you should ask the experts who were involved. I only know that it was indeed affixed, that it was placed on the launch pad, one air bomb, and that's how it was activated, just as we saw in the video-clip, by electricity. As far as I know, nothing was affixed -- nothing else was affixed to air bombs because any additional element, if you added anything else to the rocket that would have a bearing on its accuracy. The air bomb would become heavier, the elements from the table would not correspond to its properties, and it would become inaccurate. It would not hit the target. The tables did not envisage attaching anything to that air bomb, just the rocket fuel could be affixed to it and that was all that was envisaged by firing tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that video, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you know the source of it or -- and the timing, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, I do have that somewhere, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it with the understanding that they will be forthcoming later on. Let's give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's Exhibit P5982.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, just a little guidance on the timing of the break. Do you want to go till 12.30 and then -- or do you want [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much -- I'm sorry, I was overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I won't finish by 12.30 in any event, so I'm entirely in the Court's hands on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take a break at 12.30 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- if it is okay with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. So, Colonel, I understand that you don't have any particular understanding of or grip on the use of air bombs that involved more than one rocket? You don't deny that that -- that those were used; you're just not familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the use of a single rocket stuck into the back end of an air bomb, let me ask you this question: Is it your position that -- well, first of all, before I get to that, let me ask you something about the optical -- the built-in sighting mechanism that you referred to and the lack of deviation from any elements. Now, I'm not sure precisely what you were referring to as the built-in sighting mechanism because that may involve a term of art. Are you referring to the device that's affixed to, for example, both a mortar at the top of the tripod and also a rocket-launching system so that the firing table calculations can be -- so you can adjust the elevation of the launcher accordingly?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. The sighting mechanism is for aiming at targets; without it, you would just shoot, aim for nothing. We had a sighting mechanism in order to hit the target. We wanted not only to fire the bomb but also to hit the target. That's why there was sighting mechanisms. You could -- they were similar to sighting mechanisms on a mortar. You could apply elements to them, you could set your target, and there were devices like on the classical mechanisms on the lower part of the launcher to adjust the elevation and to adjust the trajectory. I don't have to be familiar with any specific weapons, but when I come to a new weapon, when I see that it has all of those elements, when I have a trained crew, then I use that piece of weaponry just like any other classical piece of weaponry. You do your corrections and so on and so forth. The air bombs were precise, they did not deviate much, they had a rocket engine that could stabilise it throughout flight just like a rocket in a multiple-rocket launcher.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is speaking too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, interpreters were not able to keep up with you again. Could you slow down and repeat your question -- repeat your answer, please. From -- they stopped after they translated you saying that: "The air bombs were precise, they did not deviate much, they had a rocket engine that could stabilise it throughout flight, just like a rocket in a multiple-rocket launcher."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters. I'm trying to speak slowly; however, they were accurate, as I have just told you, because they had rocket engines and stabilisers that they had allowed them a stable flight. There were no -- there were no deviations in trajectory, just like in rockets that were launched from multiple-rocket launchers. When it came to distance, it had a similar dispersion picture as a rocket. It -- targets were over-targeted or short-targeted but not much. The deviations were marginal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that the second element -- there are two targeting elements, one is distance and the other is direction, and I don't see that this has been recorded properly. The direction has not been recorded properly. It was omitted from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say that, Mr. Simic, those two elements, distance and direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I was talking about direction where there were marginal deviations, if any at all, and there were also marginal deviations when it came to distance so the target could be either short-targeted or over-targeted but only marginally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So the process with the air bombs that you assert you're familiar with, that is, the ones where the rocket was screwed into the back end of an air bomb, was that the -- the relative co-ordinates of the target would be identified, then someone would open up the rocket firing tables to find out the elevation that should be used to achieve that distance, then would use that device you talked about to elevate the launcher to the correct number of mils as indicated by the rocket firing table, and then it would be fired or perhaps some directional adjustment could be made as well. Is that basically it?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you're not suggesting that the addition of a -- an air bomb to a rocket would somehow improve its precision and accuracy; you're just suggesting that it didn't make any appreciable difference?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. If I understood you properly a while ago and if things were interpreted properly to me, I explained that when something is attached to an air bomb and -- the only thing that is attached to it is a rocket engine which propels it to take it to the target, nothing else. And the firing tables had been prepared in advance and based on the quantity of the fuel that has to propel the air bomb to a certain distance and that's the elevation that you take. Based on the weight of the air bomb, that's how you decide the quantity of the fuel or the gunpowder that has to propel it to the target. Nothing else is attached to it but the rocket engine that propels it to the target. I don't what else. What I'm saying is that nothing else is attached to the air bomb but the rocket engine which is necessary to launch the air bomb in the first place. I don't know what you're saying in your question. Why are you saying that something else is affixed or attached to it? I don't know if anything else is attached to it or --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Stop, please. Stop. You don't have to ask rhetorical questions. We can get this straightened out very quickly. It's not the bomb itself that has a firing table because it's normally dropped out of an airplane, right; it's rocket that has a firing table?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. However, in view of the situation that we discussed just a while ago, we -- I told you how we launched it. It could not just be launched arbitrarily. All the other elements had to be provided in advance in order to launch an air bomb. You had to have firing tables, and those firing tables are made by experts. I was not involved in compiling firing tables so I wouldn't know what they entailed. But just like any other artillery weapons experts are familiar with the type of shells, you determine distances for a certain type of ammunition, there are firing tables for every artillery weapon. And that's how things were done for air bombs as well. That was done subsequently when those launchers were crafted, and when launching of air bombs started in that way, firing tables were devised. They were compiled, they had to be prepared in advance because everything else would have been just shooting blindly, shooting in the air, I don't know where. Firing tables were compiled in order to hit the target and they accompanied every piece of weaponry, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you ever see one of these firing tables?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on those two occasions -- actually on just one occasion. The first time I saw those firing tables, I saw how elements were calculated and applied to the weapon that was used on the Nisici plateau.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was it a Plamen? Oganj? Grad? Or another firing table?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A firing table for Plamen whose rocket weighs 21 or 22 kilogrammes and had a rocket propellant cannot correspond to a bomb that weighs 220 kilogrammes or any other. I don't know how experts calculated all that, but I saw special firing tables for that particular launcher that was used there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I see the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's about time to take a break, but can I ask how much longer would you need to conclude your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Estimating 30 to 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I just noted that you spent more than four hours, which you estimated, just for information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I noted that as well. It's one of the reasons I was -- I repeatedly noted that -- it was not to be impolite but to note that the witness did have a tendency to speak on for a period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.31 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The proceedings have been delayed due to technical difficulties again. There are a couple of matters that I'd like to deal with before we go further in the absence of the witness. First, in relation to the witness after the next one, i.e., Dusan Zurovac, the Chamber notes the following. The Chamber has received three signed versions of the witness's statements dated respectively the 2nd, the 5th, and the 9th of November. The first of these signed statements made reference to 11 associated exhibits, the second to 20 exhibits, and the third to 29 exhibits. None of the nine additional associated exhibits sought for admission in the third version of the statement are on the accused's 65 ter list. The third version of the statement also adds 12 short paragraphs related to scheduled incidents F4 and F10. The Chamber is concerned that the accused's Defence team met with the witness three times over the course of one week to produce three signed statements, adding new material along the way and even after the date when the witness was scheduled to testify. The accused's explanation in the latest Rule 92 ter notification that "revisions were made necessary by the discovery of additional documents and information concerning the area of the witness's responsibility" is not sufficient or satisfactory. It is incumbent on the Defence team to provide one signed statement which reflects the evidence the witness will provide. This practice of producing multiple signed versions of a witness statement is not an adequate use of the Defence team's time and resources. The Chamber also notes that a large portion of the witness's statement relates to Mostar, a municipality not covered in the indictment, and to crimes committed by Serbs; it also touches upon the witness's publications in relation to "his research concerning the suffering of the Serbs in BiH." Accordingly, the Chamber orders that Dusan Zurovac be led live only on matters related to this indictment. Next matter is related to the ICMP and I can deal with in public session. Mr. Robinson, I note that your motion for a binding order against the ICMP is still pending before the Chamber and that we are still waiting to hear from you on the final results of the ICMP's inquiries with the family members of the victims regarding disclosure of their genetic data. I also note that the last we heard on that is your e-mail to the ICMP on the 20th of September, 2012, in which you referred to 30 cases awaiting consent. Since it is now November, I wonder if you can tell us what the update on that is and whether you have received the final numbers from the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. I received a communication from the ICMP about ten days ago, in which they advised us that they had made some progress. They provided additional material and I believe that the number of cases in which they have not yet resolved is still about a dozen or less. So they're -- and they promised that they would be trying to conclude those within a short period of time. So I definitely have it on my list of things to do, that as soon as they give me the final numbers and the final information, I'm going to advise the Chamber in writing about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is something I would like to say, Your Honours, but in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are -- I think we are open session, but due to technical difficulties the -- on the monitor, the "private session" logo may appear. And I have to correct my reading of the transcript. Let me check. At page 65 , line 22, I think I misread. It should read "crimes committed to the Serbs." Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, with all due respect, I have to say that I have to prepare for submission. I am under the impression that I'm not being treated fairly. The restrictions imposed on the Defence are far greater than those that were imposed on the Prosecution. Above all, with regard to context, the Prosecution submitted documents and elements from municipalities that are no longer included in the indictment. I can't do that and, furthermore, I haven't been granted protective measures for certain witnesses. This makes the situation a lot more difficult. And in the case of crimes committed against the Serbs, this is particularly the case. I'm not saying this as a tu quoque remark, but it has to do with the context and the understanding the civil war. Not everything was done under my command. Events followed their own order, so my concern is such that I really have to make a submission to you in regard to this issue. I believe that the restrictions imposed on the Defence are far greater than those imposed on the Prosecution. On the other hand, the Prosecution has been position to threaten the witnesses simply by showing them or referring to Rule 92(E) -- or 90(E), rather, simply by virtue of interrogating witnesses to whom it was said that they were suspects. So there is no possibility of there being parity between the Defence and the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm stopping you here, but it's not appropriate to discuss it in a vacuum. We'll deal with it as it arises during the course of your examination. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, before we do that I have a few matters I would like to also put on the record. First of all, you issued a decision on the Prosecution's interviews of Defence witnesses on the 8th of November, 2012, which in paragraph 14 you directed the Prosecution to give timely notice to the accused of witnesses that it wishes to interview to give us an opportunity to speak to those witnesses, which we appreciate. However, we were informed by the Prosecution on Friday, the day after you issued this order, that it had contacted already one of the witnesses without giving us advanced notice and the Prosecution indicated that that was inadvertent and they were the ones who brought that to our attention, and we fully accept that representation. However, I wanted to put it on the record and ask Mr. Tieger to make sure that all members of the Prosecution, not only in his team but any other teams that might have any potential need to contact these witnesses, to comply with the Trial Chamber's order. Secondly, Mr. President, you issued on the 1st of November, 2012, the decision on the accused's motion for protective measures for witnesses KW289, KW299, KW378, and KW543, and I wanted to put on the record that after being informed that their requests for protective measures had been denied, witnesses KW299 and KW543 declined to testify and will not be called. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I say another thing about the witness who is to appear. Your Excellencies, I asked for time from the beginning of the 1st of March and I'm not free so I can't speak to the witness in a timely fashion. I only have access to the witness once the witness appears to testify. All my investigators don't know all the things that I know when you put all their knowledge together. They don't know what I have to ask the witness about. I'd like some flexibility with regard to this. I'm still receiving 66(B) rule documents. When am I going to integrate all of this into my strategy, go over all of this? Could you please consider this again? I should have sufficient room to update everything when seeing the witness because I don't have sufficient time. I'm trying to calculate how many witnesses I'll be able to call and I'll be spending matters that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we're not going there. But just simply speaking for myself, you have to accept some consequences of your decision to represent yourself, and it's absolutely not necessary for you to proof every and each witness. We'll just leave it at that. Shall we bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given that the third session was delayed to start at ten to 2.00, unless there's a serious objection from the parties the Chamber is minded to sit till 20 past 3.00. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and we'll try to move as quickly as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, I had asked you a question earlier that I believe was -- well, it was clearly misunderstood so let me try again because that will get us right into the subject -- one of the last subjects I'd like to address with you and that was the following. First of all, the air bomb delivery system that we've discussed was dependent upon the rockets for propulsion; correct? I'm just taking a step at a time.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firing air bombs - not aircraft bombs, that's something else - that depended on the rocket engine. The rocket engine consisted of the rocket fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. That -- as we discussed before, the underlying rocket that was used for the purpose of this propulsion, without with regard to the science of how the rocket propelled itself and the air bomb along with it, had a certain inherent accuracy to it even before it was affixed to the air bomb; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I have already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And my simple question - at least I hope simple question - is that the inherent accuracy of that rocket was not going to be improved by the -- by being affixed to the air bomb; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. The rocket, the air bomb -- I said that when you attach a rocket engine to the air bomb and the rocket engine consists of the gunpowder charge which makes it possible to launch it to hit the target -- well, that's what I said. There's nothing to be improved. I don't understand the question. I have explained this on several occasions. It's not a rocket of any kind. All I said is that the air bomb became a rocket as of the time that a rocket engine was attached to it. It's not a rocket. It's turned into a rocket because it has a rocket engine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We saw in the video pre-existing rockets which were screwed into the back of an air bomb and you agreed that was one of the mechanisms of delivery for air bombs; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, that isn't a rocket; it's a rocket engine. There is a difference. The rocket consists of the rocket engine and the charge. The charge was in the air bomb in this case and the rocket engine is the gunpowder that is used for the charge in the shell and it delivers the shell to the target. That's the rocket. A war head with an explosive charge and a rocket engine, that's it. There's no rocket here. The rocket consists of the war head and the rocket engine. I think I've been clear. I don't know else I could explain this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, the accuracy of a rocket such as a Plamen or Oganj or a Grad is not dependent upon the charge, it's dependent upon the rocket system, isn't it? So I'm not talking about the charge, I'm talking about the rocket.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally. The precision of any rocket depends on the charge, the amount of charge that is used. In places where the ammunition is produced, tables are made. You measure the quantity of gunpowder in grams, it's even more precise. It depends on the rocket engine. For example, if you have 2 kilogrammes and 2 and a half grams of gunpowder in the rocket engine -- well, that's not okay. You don't -- that doesn't correspond to the firing tables. In places where the ammunition is produced, you have to precisely measure the gunpowder charge. In this case, you have a sort of rod form of gunpowder so that it burns more slowly and because the weight is greater. This is done so the air bomb can reach its target. And in the case of the Plamen multiple-rocket launcher and the Oganj, you also used this rod charge and not powder -- not a powder charge. I think I've been clear. So it all depends, you can't just use any kind of powder as a charge so that everything is in accordance with the firing tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So your position is that rockets use various charges just like mortars or howitzers to determine the distance they'll travel?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: All right. Let's -- apart from that, let me try once more with the previous question, and if that's not successful, I'll move on to something slightly different. Irrespective of how you consider the rocket works, do you -- well, I'm going to move on to something else. You've already told us that in your view, the dispersion of the air bombs that were attached to these rocket engines was essentially the same as the underlying rocket systems themselves. So I'd like to look at the firing table for one of those underlying systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So if we could turn, please, to 65 ter 24036. This is a firing table for a Vulkan or a Grad system, and if we could turn quickly to page 5 of the -- 6 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S. No, I'm sorry, it's page 5 of the English. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we be told whose instructions these are, from which army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can say at the moment. What I do know is that both the Grad and the -- this is applicable to both because you have both the Russian system of calculation of mils and the European system and you have calculations for both the Grad and the Vulkan which are essentially identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That indicates at page 5, Colonel, that the use of these projectiles, which are identified here by their technical number, for distances up to 5 kilometres is "possible in extraordinary cases and only in situations where there are no friendly troops in the direction of fire since a significant amount of short rounds are possible caused by a large dispersal of the projectile at these ranges."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Next I'd like to look at some of the specific firing table range of error data available, and in that connection I'd like to look at B/C/S page 12 and we can identify the specific -- if we can blow that up, please, and just have that on a single page. Okay. At the top of the page we see "daljinar" for the range finder both at 1 to 6.000 which would be for the Grad and 1 to 6400 for the Vulkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we look to the immediate -- to the right, Colonel, I think you can see "po daljini" and "po provcu" so you can see error by distance and error by direction. And why don't we scroll down, for example, to -- as you can see at 1600 we have 250 metres by distance, 9.2 by direction. And if we go down to 5.000, for example, at the next page, and we can see it descending that way. A slight decrease in the error by distance and an increase in the error by direction. So at 5.000, we have 215 metres by distance and 29 by direction. Now, first of all, Colonel, can you confirm that these -- that this range of error is -- does not refer to the diameter of the error but to the radius, that is, it essentially is that figure on either side of the intended target. So in the case of 5.000 metres, it would be 215 metres by direction short or long and 29 metres by direction to either side.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with these firing tables. I'm not familiar with the Grad or the Vulkan system either, but as a rule, the firing tables look something like this. In the firing tables there are certain deviations for the distance and for the direction when you fire at a certain distance. As you increase the range, these errors, this range of errors, also increases. When you fire the first projectile, this is taken into account. It was quite small, but as you said multiple-rocket launchers and air bombs had greater deviations in the distance than in direction. You mentioned 200, 250 metres with regard to the distance and 20 to 30 metres with regard to the direction. So 20, 30 metres is not a huge error for such an air bomb with such a destructive capacity. I think that as a rule firing tables were compiled in this way, but I'm not familiar with these weapons, but these adjustments are taken into consideration when projectiles are fired and this is the purpose for which firing tables are used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Colonel. Are you also aware that the firing table figures discount the extreme -- because when firing tables are assembled based on many, many, many tests, they discard the most extreme firings and try to identify a range of error within sort of a middle ground, in the top 50 per cent, for example. You're nodding so it appears you're aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that firing tables are compiled based on a number of test shots in order to establish an average. I don't know how averages are established, but I know that these tables are based on trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you know that to establish a useful figure, many, many, many trials are required to come up with a meaningful average?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, firing tables are not compiled by crews who work on the launchers. It is professionals who are trained for that who do that because there is a series of parameters that have a bearing on the validity of a firing table which will be produced for use in various conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, there's absolutely no basis for tendering the document with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Why would that be? I think there's an ample basis for doing so, but I can lay a further foundation if necessary. The witness talked about whether or not rockets were or should be used in certain conditions, he talked about the relationship between the rockets and the air bombs. These -- this data would be admissible on either ground, and certainly in light of the fact that both of those factors are relevant here, these tables are also relevant in addition to the general discussion that took place about the table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did the witness lay some foundation on this document, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have not told us yet --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He recognised -- yes, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, we haven't heard yet where this document was from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's a firing table produced by the Croatian government in response to an RFA, so therefore reflecting systems used in the former JNA and in the various military establishments that developed thereafter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. -- I'm sorry to interrupt Mr. Karadzic, but I see there's an ambiguity in what I said. I didn't mean it was produced by the Croatian government. I meant we made an RFA to the Croatian government and we received this in response. This is a JNA firing table to the best of our understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I remember properly, the witness said that he was not familiar with these systems. He said that this is the way that tables are compiled; however, the figures contained in these particular tables mean nothing to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, first of all -- let me lay further foundation, then. First of all, not that I think it's necessary, but first of all, the witness did affirm, as I think is very obvious, that this is a firing table and a type of firing table that he is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Sorry to interrupt. Why don't you put those questions to the witness so that we can get some foundation of this document from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, you still have that in front of you. You've used firing tables in the past, I take it, and in particular in connection with rockets. I know you had rocket experience from actually the earliest phase of your JNA career.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I used firing tables for the weapons that I used and on which I was trained and on which I trained my subordinates. At the beginning of my career, I was the commander of a battery of multi-rocket launchers Plamen and I had the firing tables. These are not JNA firing tables, they would be in Serbian. This is Croatian, pure Croatian, as far as I can tell, but it's neither here nor there. I said that in principle this is what firing tables normally look like, and this particular firing table applies to the kinds of weapons that I'm not familiar with. When I was in the JNA, I never heard of these types of weapons nor did I see them during the war. I still don't know what Vulkan looks like, or Grad. I only heard that Grad looks like the Oganj multiple-rocket launcher, that it is mobile, mounted on a vehicle; however, I've never had an opportunity to see one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we -- you're aware of the fact, however, that Grad rockets were used extensively in the air bomb production process, that is, the VRS air bomb production process?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, for the umpteenth time I repeat, Grad rocket and air bombs, I didn't say that they were used. I don't know where Grad rockets were used, in what part of the theatre of war. If we at all had that type of rockets, I never saw them. Rockets on the one hand and air bombs on the other, I've already said rockets and air bombs have nothing to do with each other. I have told you that an air bomb becomes a rocket with an engine, with a gunpowder charge. This is an air bomb and the rocket engine propels it to its target. This is the -- all I can say. I have no other explanation. There is no rocket that is attached to an air bomb. Gunpowder rod is attached to the rocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it -- I'm getting a little far afield and moving into my next questions, but in any event I think the witness's answers previously are sufficient to justify the admission of this firing table.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we ask Mr. Tieger to ask the witness to read from the left upper corner what kind of charge is in question here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think that's necessary at the moment. I'll consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, now we did hear you object to the application for admission, but we didn't get the grounds of objection. May we have them, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President -- Judge Baird. I don't mean to elevate you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: The grounds are simply that the witness hasn't confirmed anything about this document, so he doesn't know about this -- these rockets and he isn't capable of confirming whether these firing tables are accurate, whether they're applicable to the weapons that the VRS had or used. And so absent that kind of foundation, in line with your previous guide-lines that you've been following throughout the whole trial, this doesn't fall within a document that can be admitted through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May I respond to that because I think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The Chamber has another question for you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, even if this document was admitted, what practical use is it going to be to the Trial Chamber, other than the fact it is a document we've not been asked to nor would we seek to use the figures and the calculations in it because they are not relevant to any evidence we've heard --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That -- I'm sorry, Judge Morrison, I didn't realise you weren't finished. That's precisely the point. I wanted to respond in connection with that underlying point to something raised by Mr. Robinson, which is to say that the -- it's -- this can't be admitted unless it's shown that they're applicable to the weapons the VRS had or used. This is not an abstract document and Mr. -- we have noted throughout that when it serves the purpose of general impeachment, it's certainly sufficient to note that this document is what it purports to be. In connection with the assertion that we don't have evidence to that effect, I was a bit surprised to hear that since paragraph 155 of 1D25159, an expert report submitted by the Defence, refers to the modified aircraft bombs, "bearing in mind that the components fitted into the system FAB-150 and 250 aircraft bombs and 122-millimetre Grad rocket motors had been manufactured," et cetera, et cetera. It was the Defence in part which placed this very squarely at issue and made it relevant, and that's precisely one of the ways in which the Court should be entitled to use this firing table in assessing the use of the air bombs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you not produce that -- this firing table when Mr. -- Dr. Subotic is going to testify?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I believe I could, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But it seemed to be entirely relevant right now talking to a commander who told the Court about the impropriety of using -- the underlying rockets in urban areas and now talked about the precision of air bombs which we know depended upon those underlying systems. And so I thought it was quite relevant for the Court to have that information and available to it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the Chamber is not satisfied that this witness has given sufficient foundation about this document to be admitted at the moment. In addition, I note that this was not translated in full, but that's not the reason for postponing the admission. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, if I could just take this opportunity for a moment to ask the Trial Chamber to consider imposing some time-limits on the Prosecution's cross-examination so that we have some parity and Dr. Karadzic alluded to this. We are feeling here on the Defence side that there is sometimes decisions of the Trial Chamber that disadvantage us vis-a-vis the Prosecution. And you wanted him to be specific. So this is a very specific example of a cross-examination that has taken 10 to 20 times the length of the direct examination and which exceeded the estimate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, I'll cut you off here. The Chamber expressly stated that it will monitor the conduct of the trial for some time, and as for the Prosecution case, the Defence was at liberty in terms of amount of cross-examination for the first phase of the proceeding. It took some time to impose time constraint -- restraint to the Defence after -- yes, it took a while since the start of the Prosecution case to start imposing some time-limit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, by calling this to your attention, I hope you'll consider this for the future depending on how things evolve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I guarantee the Chamber is more keen to the overall time of the proceedings. Thank you. Let's move on, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And in the interests of time, I'm not responding to what I consider to be an unfair and specious objection, but I'll move right on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I have just a few very discrete areas to cover. First of all, at page 55 I had asked you earlier about your own involvement with air bombs one way or another and you said you weren't involved in any shape or form with air bombs. And in that connection I wanted to call up P1300. Okay. This is a document dated the 11th of July, 1995. It refer -- is sent to various brigades discussing the needs of the corps and orders that the above-mentioned units shall issue a FAB 250 and 105 kilogrammes to Major Simic on July 12th as follows, it lists them, and it says then: "Major Simic shall obtain 2 aerial bombs of 250 kilogrammes from the corps reserve which are currently located ..." et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. He "shall prepare the deployment plan for the air bomb launcher and make all preparations for the action according to the 'Talas 1' plan." Colonel, I put it to you that your answer about not being involved in any way, shape or form, or any shape or form in air bombs was not accurate and the claim -- and the fact that you were involved in air bombs explains your insistence on their alleged precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to object, Mr. President. That's another one of Dr. Karadzic's sins of multiple questions within one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Major, you were involved with air bombs despite your claim to this Trial Chamber not very long ago that you were not involved in any shape or form; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you can see from this document that General Milosevic ordered me to take over air bombs and deploy them across the brigades that had launchers. I was supposed to take them over and distribute them. Under 2, you can see -- or rather, under 3, you can see that: "Major Simic shall prepare the deployment plan for the a/b launcher and make all preparations for the action according to the 'Talas 1' plan." I would like to see that Talas 1 order. I don't know what that refers to. I've done a lot of things from -- I did a lot of things from 1992 to 1995. I can't remember all the details. If I saw this plan, I could tell you what it applies to, but if there was a plan, it doesn't mean that it was ever acted upon. I stated that I observed the actions of air bombs on two occasions, I mentioned what the targets were. I'm not contesting that I may have been involved in the planning and delivery of those air bombs. If I had taken them over from a certain position, then I may have deployed them upon the order of the corps commander to the specific brigades. I would like to see the Talas 1 order to see what that order applies to. I don't remember. That was at a time when the Muslim offensive was taking place in the Sarajevo theatre of war in 1995 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Colonel, you are venturing far afield from the question I asked. Two final matters. In paragraphs 29, 30 -- basically 30 through 32, you offer certain views on Markale I and Markale II, basically to the effect that both incidents involved, in your view, an individual shot without adjusted fire and therefore it was impossible that the shell which landed could have been fired by the Bosnian Serb side; correct? You don't have to repeat it. I'm just using that as a predicate. That's the position you take in your statement; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I claim that Markale I and II could not be hit by a mortar shell fired from any of the Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So it's your position that a -- that single shots into Sarajevo don't have any possibility of hitting their intended target; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my statement I stated even if we were to assume that the target was hit by a mortar shell, it could not have been done from the first go. The first shell fired from any position could not have hit that target. Second of all, even if that first shell had hit the target of Markale, knowing how large the market-place is, I'm sure that any artillery -- no artillerymen could see the market from his observation post. This would have been a blind shot. After the smoke appeared after the explosion, it would have appeared somewhere else carried by wind. So that shot would have been unreliable. It would have not been accurate. Let's assume that the first shot had hit the target. We could not have observed it. There's no observation post anywhere from which you could see the Markale market. I still claim that the first shot could not hit that target. On the assumption that it had hit the market, which I claim it didn't, but if it had, it would have gone unobserved from any of our observers on any of our observation posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I take it you take the position that any single shot, any single random shot into Sarajevo has no military purpose because it's not going to hit a -- its intended target, that the person firing it doesn't know where it's going to land?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not what I am claiming. I am talking specifically about the Markale market. It's a small market between various buildings, among buildings, those buildings are very high. And I told you, even if the first shell had hit that target, it would have gone unobserved. Second of all, for a shell to land within such a small area among the buildings, it should have been fired from a shorter distance because of the angle. The angle has to be at least 85 degrees, so the angle had to be almost vertical in order for that shell to land among the buildings in that small area which could not be observed from any of the Serbian observation posts. This is what I'm saying. I'm not saying that any individual shell fired during the war was just a randomly fired shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Last brief topic I wanted to raise with you arises out of paragraph 25 when you say: "The incident of 27 May 1992, in Vase Miskina Street was explained to me ..." And that's preceded by the words "incident G1." How did you know -- what made you think that the incident of 27 May 1992 in Vase Miskina Street was incident G1? Did you see that somewhere or did someone tell you that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that by the Defence team. They told me that it was the G-1 incident. I don't know why it was marked that way. That's how it was marked. I don't know why, based on what. It's just known as G-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What was it marked on?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear you properly or perhaps I didn't understand you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, who marked it and what was it marked on?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I provided my statement, when I provided my statement about the incident which is known as G-1 in Vase Miskina Street, I provided my opinion about that incident and that was marked as G-1. I don't know why. I don't know how. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I take it you did not look at the indictment to see that G-1 is an incident that took place on or about the 28th of May and that, in fact, whoever told you it was G-1 on the Defence did not accurately advise you that the Vase Miskina Street incident is not included in the indictment, as Dr. Karadzic himself noted at T6394 through 95.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I was asked to provide a statement about the incident in Vase Miskina Street. I did provide a statement. I don't know how it was marked. I did not have an occasion or the need to get familiar with the indictment; therefore, I don't know what it contains.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellencies. Could we look at P1041.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we are waiting, Colonel, sir, did you hear from the Defence team about Vase Miskina for the first time or had you heard about it before?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it before immediately after the event. I watched the Muslim television and I saw the images on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, did you take some investigative measures in order to establish what had happened?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I was a battery commander. I don't know what the corps command did at the time. I know that requests were made to check whether fire was ever opened from our positions, from our mortars. This is as much as I can remember. I was a battery commander for a battery of multi-rocket launchers and I don't know how the investigation evolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This document was shown to you by Mr. Tieger; however, he did not show you the entire document. First of all, could you please tell us where are the speakers? Where are the people who were intercepted in this conversation? What about this unknown male person, if you look at the last line of the intercept?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unknown male person, Marsal Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move to the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we are waiting, can you tell us what was happening with Marsal Tito barracks at the time? Have a look at the top. What is Mladic being informed of? What are the Muslim media conveying?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: NN, unidentified male person, he says: "They say that the Marsal Tito barracks is carrying out a break through. That's probably the media. "General Mladic: Okay. "Unidentified male: Blow up the bridge, the Bratstvo-Jedinstvo bridge. "Mladic: Do not worry. They dare not come close to the Brotherhood and Unity Bridge or the barracks."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a look at the bottom, third line from below, from the bottom, let's see what Mladic says there.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "You too can," is that what you have in mind? "You can take more than they can. I don't want to kill the people or to destroy the town. I don't want innocent people to come to harm. If anyone wants to open fire, he should stay in Sarajevo and should let the army take positions. They should pull out the civilians, and if they want a fight, we'll fight. It would be better to fight somewhere in the hills than in town."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And it says "the people have to live somewhere," that's stated down below; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have a look at the first line. What does Mladic say there? Could you read that out?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We aren't in favour of a fight. We are in favour of peace. If they want peace, they will have it; if they don't, well, that's not a problem, we can always go to war."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, how does this intercept tally with the information you had and with your experience?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, at that time the Tito barracks was besieged, it was completely surrounded, and pressure was exerted on the men in the barracks and the barracks was preparing to leave, for an agreement to leave, to abandon -- not the barracks, I mean the troops were preparing to leave the Tito barracks. As far as I can remember, it was around June that the men left the Marsal Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see D207.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this intercept has also been shown to you, the one we're waiting for now. And another one was shown to you that relates to this one. Could we see the last three lines. Could you read it out, please.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. "Mladic: Look, they want to attack the barracks in order to provoke us to take action on the town."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, could we see the English version, page 2 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please continue, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Potpara: Yes, very well. "Mladic: Tell the people so that the people are aware of this."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have a look at page number 4, page number 8 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just for clarification, this is not an intercept, to the best of my recollection, that was shown to the witness previously.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I corrected myself. I said an intercept that relates to the one that you were shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Number, or rather, page 8 in the English, the third line from the bottom, Mladic intervenes and can we see what Potpara says.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Ah, we won't take any risks, we won't risk people's lives. "Mladic: I am of the same opinion. If they want peace, they'll have peace. Last night I issued an order as soon as I arrived ... there was this large-scale attack against the units and you. I somehow managed to calm the people down in that shooting and to place things under control to prevent action from being taken. What they're producing now, they probably have some sort of mime artists or some sort of good imitators that makes it possible for them to successfully imitate my voice, your voice, and everyone else's voice."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the next two pages -- or the next two lines.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next two lines. "Mladic: It seems that they're creating a farce down there, they're deceiving their people about some sort of commands of mine -- well, no, that's out of the question." And then Mladic says: "Let them deceive their people. You should convey this from soldier to soldier. They shouldn't play around and put their lives at risk. No one had a reserve life. We won't fire on the town. If they don't violate the agreement, if they don't threaten you, but be extremely careful. Don't trust them at all."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. How does this fit in with your experience of the VRS in relation to the town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is about the fact that orders were issued to members of units in the Tito barracks and in the town of Sarajevo, orders according to which they shouldn't expose themselves to provocations by the Muslim forces, they should exercise restraint, they should preserve the lives of their subordinates, they should be cautious and observe the situation because they couldn't trust the other side. This was proved on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we briefly see P1518, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, while waiting for that to appear, tell us what is the purpose of observing fire?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, the purpose of observing fire is to observe the target and action taken against the target in order to adjust firing so that one could fire on the target with as much precision as possible so as not to waste shells, to disperse shells, and inflict harm on civilians and civilian facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the next page, please. I apologise. That's not the one. I've mixed them up. Engage in artillery observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can observation be brought into line with random fire?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all. If you're observing artillery fire, then random fire is out of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see D192, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
